strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper convincingly argues that continual recommendation differs from conventional continual learning (stability should mean preserving long-term predictive preferences, not performance on past tasks), and supports this with an empirical analysis (Table 1) showing that cumulative LoRA designs transfer poorly from user-disjoint to natural chronological splits.

The proposed PESO method is simple, principled, and efficient: a single evolving LoRA with a proximal (L2 or softmax-KL) anchor to the previous adapter state, with O(1) storage versus O(T) for cumulative LoRA and negligible computational overhead.

Theory is clean and well-integrated: Proposition 1 (direction-wise interpolation between the new optimum and previous adapter via generalized eigenpairs of the tangent-feature second-moment), Corollary 2 (data-aware stability-plasticity gating), and Proposition 3/Corollary 4 (softmax-KL locally quadratic, interpretable as p-weighted variance) provide genuine intuition for why the method works, with full proofs in the appendix.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three Amazon categories plus Yelp, multiple baselines (single evolving LoRA, a carefully ablated cumulative LoRA family with SumLoRA/SD-LoRA/InfLoRA variants, O-LoRA, AM-LoRA, LSAT, full fine-tuning, full retraining, and traditional two-tower continual recommenders), ablations over regularizer choices and λ, backbone robustness (LC-REC), drift quantification, dormant/new-user analysis, and explicit forgetting measurement (Table 12).

PESO consistently ranks best across nearly all metrics and datasets, with sensible analyses (e.g., selective benign forgetting, learning-rate scaling with block size) that go beyond just reporting wins.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea—proximal regularization (L2-SP/EWC-style penalties) toward the previous parameter state—is well established in continual learning; the contribution is essentially instantiating this within LoRA for generative recommenders, plus a softmax-KL variant whose local quadratic form follows directly from the known softmax Hessian. The theory, while clean, is standard linearization + quadratic analysis.

Absolute performance gains are small (e.g., NDCG@5 improvements of ~0.001–0.0015 over the best baselines), and no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported across the (apparently single) runs, making it hard to judge robustness of the margins.

Evaluation protocol has some issues: metrics are averaged over D2–D4 although the data defines stages up to D5 (stage 5 appears unused in main results); leave-one-out with only one test item and a single backbone (Llama-3.2 1B) in the main table limits generality; the main-table comparison to the authors' own re-derived baseline variants (e.g., SumLoRA latest+inherit) is somewhat bespoke.

Some inconsistencies and sloppiness: RQ list announces four questions but lists five (RQ5); Table 4 is an abbreviated duplicate of Table 6; the abstract's code link is empty; occasional typos ('expected too work well', 'matrcies').

The 'natural chronological' setting is close to ordinary sequential fine-tuning, and the cumulative-LoRA strawman analysis, while informative, is conducted largely with the authors' own constructed variants; stronger external validation (e.g., established continual-rec benchmarks) would bolster the claims.

The conceptual stability-plasticity model in Appendix A (Eq. 15) is informal and not empirically validated, and the interpretation of eigenvectors as 'decoupled preference axes' (Appendix B.3) is speculative.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies and motivates a real distinction between continual recommendation and standard continual learning (stability should preserve only predictive long-term preferences, not outdated ones), which is a useful reframing of the stability-plasticity trade-off.

The empirical analysis in Section 3 (Table 1), which dissects the cumulative LoRA family under user-disjoint vs. natural chronological splits and shows the original cumulative design degrades under cross-stage interference, is a genuine and informative contribution that contextualizes the proposed method.

The experimental coverage is broad: three Amazon categories plus Yelp, two LLM backbones, multiple cumulative LoRA variants (SumLoRA, SD-LoRA, InfLoRA), additional continual PEFT baselines (O-LoRA, AM-LoRA, LSAT), full fine-tuning/retraining comparisons, drift-score quantification, dormant/new-user analysis for stability-plasticity, hyperparameter sensitivity, and efficiency analysis.
The theory is correctly stated and clearly written; Proposition 1 and Corollary 2 give an interpretable direction-wise interpolation view, and the proofs in Appendix B are complete.
The writing and organization are clear, and the problem is practically relevant to LLM-based generative recommenders.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method. Anchoring new parameters to previous parameters with a proximal penalty is a classic idea (EWC, L2-SP, and function-space distillation variants), and applying it to a single evolving LoRA is a fairly direct combination. The softmax-KL instantiation is the only new ingredient, and it is ad hoc: applying softmax to raw, arbitrarily scaled LoRA factor entries has no clear semantic justification, and the 'per-module structure' argument is weak. O-LoRA and output-level KL already cover much of this design space.

The theory is elementary and rests on strong, possibly unrealistic assumptions: a single linearization at theta_0 held fixed across all stages, a fixed LoRA subspace U = [I_m 0], an MSE surrogate for cross-entropy, and a quadratic approximation of the loss. The main result reduces to ridge-regression shrinkage in a rotated basis; it does not rigorously distinguish PESO from L2 or EWC-style alternatives, and the local-quadratic analysis of softmax-KL (Proposition 3) is a straightforward Taylor expansion.

Empirical gains are small and reported without uncertainty. Absolute NDCG values are around 0.01-0.03, and relative improvements over the strongest baselines are often only 1-4%, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests, making it hard to assess whether differences are reliable.

Several results undercut the central narrative but are not adequately confronted: Table 12 shows PESO exhibits more forgetting than both baselines on most past blocks (e.g., 0.0107 vs. 0.0087/0.0062 on D1), which is explained away post hoc as 'benign forgetting'; Table 10 shows PESO has lower Hit@5 than SD-LoRA (0.0179 vs. 0.0185) yet PESO's value is bolded as best, suggesting inconsistent or favorable reporting.

Evaluation details raise concerns: metrics are averaged over D2..D4 even though five incremental blocks are defined, leaving D5's role unclear; how lambda was selected per dataset (validation vs. test) is not specified; and the comparison with dedicated continual recommenders (PISA, Contrastive+PIW) is relegated to an appendix with mixed results (PESO beats PISA only modestly and the relative-gain analysis is acknowledged to favor traditional methods).

The evaluation protocol itself (leave-one-out with beam-search generation of 10 items, no popularity debiasing, semantic IDs from a fixed tokenizer) is standard but the paper does not address known biases of generative-retrieval evaluation, and the framework is tightly coupled to a fixed item tokenizer, limiting applicability when new items arrive (acknowledged only in a footnote).

Significance: the contribution is an incremental refinement of known continual-learning regularizers for a specific setting. The impact appears confined to a narrow sub-area, and the improvements over simple strong baselines (single evolving LoRA, L2 proximal) may not justify the added complexity in practice.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper convincingly articulates why continual recommendation differs from vision-style continual learning (stability means preserving still-predictive long-term preferences, not predicting past preferences), which is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution for the sub-area.

The empirical analysis in Section 3 / Table 1 is a highlight: the design-choices ablation of the cumulative LoRA family (all vs. latest vs. inheritance variants) on natural chronological vs. pseudo user-disjoint splits directly supports the central claim that task-independent adapter aggregation is ill-suited to evolving user preferences.

The proposed method (PESO) is simple, principled, and well-motivated; the theory (Propositions 1 and 3, Corollaries 2 and 4) gives an interpretable data-aware, direction-wise interpolation account of the stability-plasticity trade-off, and full proofs are provided in the appendix.

Comprehensive and mostly convincing evaluation: three Amazon categories plus Yelp, multiple LoRA-based continual baselines (InfLoRA, SumLoRA, SD-LoRA, O-LoRA, AM-LoRA, LSAT), alternative regularizers (RQ2), dormancy/new-user analysis (RQ3), hyperparameter sensitivity (RQ4), traditional two-tower continual recommenders (RQ5), a second backbone (LC-REC), distribution-shift quantification, and efficiency analysis.
Reproducibility is addressed well: detailed data preprocessing, dataset statistics, evaluation protocol, hyperparameter search ranges, and a stated code release.

PESO consistently achieves the best or near-best results across most metrics and datasets, and the dormant/new-user analysis (Table 3) directly evidences the claimed stability-plasticity balance rather than merely reporting aggregate gains.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: proximal regularization toward a previous parameter state is closely related to well-established techniques (EWC, L2-SP, and general proximal/trust-region methods). The main methodological increment is applying a per-module softmax-KL proximal within a single evolving LoRA; the theory is competent but largely standard (quadratic surrogate + generalized eigen decomposition), and the linearization/MSE-surrogate assumptions create a noticeable gap between the analysis and the actual cross-entropy training objective.

Absolute performance gains over the strongest baselines are modest (roughly 3-6% relative), and on some metrics the improvement vanishes (e.g., 0.00% on Books H@5 vs. single evolving LoRA); with no reported variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance tests, it is hard to judge how robust these margins are.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: Table 10 shows SD-LoRA beating PESO on Hit@5 with the LC-REC backbone, yet the text states PESO 'maintains its superiority'; the abstract claims outperformance over 'existing LoRA-based continual learning methods' while several comparisons are deferred to the appendix.

Minor inconsistencies and sloppiness that reduce confidence: the text variously says results are averaged over D2,...,D5 and D2,...,D4; Table 12 references a 'D0' block never defined in the main text; typos such as 'expected too work well' and 'matrcies'.

The strongest competing design axis is only lightly explored: the analysis is confined to LoRA-level solutions, and the comparison with replay-based continual methods for the LLM recommender (a natural and possibly stronger alternative) is not included.

The theoretical 'data-aware, direction-wise guidance' depends on eigenvectors of a fixed linearization at theta0; the paper acknowledges relinearization concerns only in a remark, and the practical relevance of the eigen-direction semantics (e.g., 'sci-fi affinity' axes) is asserted intuitively rather than validated empirically.
